title: Challenges and opportunities for classroom-based formative assessment and AI: a perspective article
extended_summary:
This perspective article examines how artificial intelligence (AI) may affect classroom-based formative assessment, with particular attention to both the opportunities and the risks created by AI-enabled tools. The paper focuses on the core formative assessment cycle: eliciting evidence of learning, interpreting it, and using it to guide next instructional steps. The authors argue that while formative assessment is pedagogically valuable, it is difficult for teachers to implement consistently and at scale because of time constraints, large class sizes, feedback demands, and contextual pressures such as accountability systems and resource limitations.

The paper does not report an empirical intervention. Instead, it synthesizes prior research and uses examples such as automated essay scoring, intelligent tutoring systems, computerized formative assessment, AI-supported peer assessment, longitudinal learner profiling, and AI-assisted rubric design to illustrate how AI could support teachers and students. It also discusses practical and ethical concerns, including bias in training data, reduced interpretability of machine-learning outputs, privacy, and the possibility that AI may be over-trusted or used inappropriately. The discussion specifically notes that generative AI can help teachers generate rubric samples and feedback support, but these outputs require careful curation and human judgment.

The context is classroom formative assessment, with examples drawn from K-12 and broader education settings, including references to classroom teaching, peer assessment, and policy shifts in Australian government schools. The authors emphasize that AI should augment, not replace, teachers, and that students will need stronger self-regulated learning and critical thinking skills to use AI responsibly. They conclude with recommendations for feedback assistance, ethical use, teacher guidance, co-design research, and attention to teacher roles in interpreting AI outputs and supporting learning.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model systems used to generate text, feedback, rubrics, and other adaptive outputs for educational tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: A perspective discussion of how generative AI and related AI systems could support classroom formative assessment, including rubric generation, feedback assistance, peer-assessment prompts, and teacher support. The paper does not evaluate a specific named product beyond mentioning ChatGPT as an example.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective article with no empirical evaluation, no study design, and no reported outcomes. It discusses opportunities and risks conceptually rather than testing an AI tool in classrooms.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has potential practical relevance for K-12 formative assessment and teacher workflows, but it reports no measured effect sizes or direct impact evidence. Because impact is only argued conceptually, the tier is limited to yellow.
